title: Seventh Circuit’s Franco v. Chobani Decision Confirms That FDA Enforcement Discretion Is No Shield Against Consumer Class Actions - Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP
content:
Rachel Turow
Michael W. McTigue Jr.
Meredith C. Slawe The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit has revived a putative nationwide class action alleging that the food company Chobani deceptively marketed its Zero Sugar Greek yogurt, holding that the claims are not preempted by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA). The July 27, 2026, decision is a pointed reminder that a federal agency’s decision not to enforce its own rules, even when reviewing labeling, does not neutralize exposure under state consumer protection statutes. For food, beverage and consumer product companies that have built labeling strategies around Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance rather than formal rulemaking, Franco v. Chobani materially recalibrates the risk calculus. Under FDA regulations, a product may not be labeled “sugar free” or “zero sugar” unless it contains less than 0.5 grams of sugars as defined in 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(c)(6)(ii), which in turn defines “Total Sugars” as “the sum of all free mono- and disaccharides (such as glucose, fructose, lactose, and sucrose).” Chobani’s yogurt was marketed as sugar-free but contained 4 grams of allulose per serving. Allulose is a naturally occurring monosaccharide not listed in FDA’s regulation. The plaintiffs sued under the consumer protection laws of numerous states, and because the FDCA expressly preempts state labeling requirements that conflict with federal standards, the case turned entirely on whether allulose is a “sugar” encompassed by FDA’s regulation that lists other types of sugars. In 2020, FDA issued guidance announcing its intent to exercise enforcement discretion for the exclusion of allulose from “Total Sugars” and “Added Sugars” declarations, “pending review of the issues in a rulemaking.” That rulemaking has never occurred. The district court nevertheless treated the guidance as controlling, deferred to it under Auer and dismissed on preemption grounds. Unlike Chevron deference, which has been permanently altered by Loper Bright (see below), Auer deference calls for courts to defer to an agency’s reasonable interpretation of its own regulations. The Seventh Circuit reversed. Invited to weigh in, FDA filed an amicus brief taking the position that § 101.9(c)(6)(ii) is unambiguous and captures all monosaccharides, including allulose. Although Chobani had received approval of its zero-sugar labeling from FDA, that approval was given under the agency’s enforcement discretion policy, not its regulation. The panel agreed, reasoning that the “such as” parenthetical is illustrative rather than limiting: “The FDA defined a class by way of chemistry; it reinforced that definition through examples, all of which share the same chemical structure.” In other words, because allulose is a monosaccharide, it is a sugar that counts toward “total sugars” under FDA’s regulation. Because the plaintiffs sought to enforce standards identical to the federal ones, their claims survived preemption. The court separately held that deception was plausibly alleged, rejecting Chobani’s argument that consumers care about sugar’s health effects rather than its chemistry (allulose is not absorbed by the body in the same way as other sugars): “Whether reasonable consumers care about the existence of allulose in their yogurt isn’t the same thing as asking whether reasonable consumers would be deceived by it.” Chobani did not merely rely on generalized guidance. It obtained a temporary marketing permit that required submission of its proposed label to FDA’s Office of Nutrition, Food Labeling and Critical Foods, which demanded revisions to the allulose- and sugar-content portions and then published its approval in the Federal Register. The court was unmoved: While Chobani may reasonably have believed it was safe from federal enforcement, “the agency’s marketing permit said nothing about state law consumer protection suits,” and Chobani was “a sophisticated actor” that should have known FDA’s enforcement priorities “would not immunize the company” from state law claims. This is the familiar cycle of regulatory ambiguity in acute form. Enforcement discretion paired with the slow pace of the rulemaking process opens space for a marketing claim that may be consistent with but technically outside the letter of the law; the promised rulemaking never arrives; and the plaintiffs’ bar converts the gap between the unamended regulation and the agency’s enforcement posture into a state law deception theory. The Seventh Circuit’s decision makes this flywheel even more harrowing for food, beverage and consumer products companies because draft guidance and enforcement discretion make up the vast majority of FDA’s regulation in the food space. It is unclear how this decision would have come out under Chevron. Under the previous regime, FDA may have received more deference to its scientific view that allulose, while a monosaccharide, should be treated differently when it comes to contributing to the total sugar content of foods. But, under Loper Bright, this interpretation is a judicial task. (See our July 9, 2024, client alert “Supreme Court’s Overruling of Chevron Deference to Administrative Agencies’ Interpretations of Statutes Will Invite More Challenges to Agency Decisions.”) The court adopted its position citing Loper Bright alongside Kisor, while acknowledging that an agency’s views may still be informative under Skidmore. The practical consequence is that courts will independently determine whether informal guidance carries the force of law without deferring to the agency’s scientific judgment or rationale in all cases. FDA’s assertion that its enforcement posture should govern also carries correspondingly less weight. Notably, Franco also illustrates that an agency’s litigating position can prevail over its own published guidance. Companies that structure labeling around guidance rather than rulemaking bear that exposure. Franco binds only federal courts in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin, and other courts may reach different conclusions on preemption, enforcement discretion and questions the panel left open — including “no added sugar” claims. Chobani also preserved additional arguments for remand, including a preemption theory based on FDA’s label approval and Monsanto Co. v. Durnell. Even so, the immediate lesson is durable: Federal regulatory comfort and state law litigation risk are separate inquiries, and white space creates litigation risk. title: NFL today: How to watch Buccaneers v Cowboys, TV channels & live stream Thursday 8 October - The Guardian
content: How will the Buccaneers and Cowboys fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options The bad news for the Buccaneers: Their 0-4 start has been an unmitigated disaster that, in normal circumstances, would have already evaporated their playoff chances. The good news for Tampa Bay, however, is that they play in the NFC South, meaning they’re still just two games out of a tie for the lead in what is often the worst division in the NFL. All is not quite lost yet. If the Bucs want to join the 1992 Chargers and become the second team to make the postseason after an 0-4 opening, they’ll need to stop the bleeding on Thursday night in north Texas. They’ll have to do it without Baker Mayfield, who continues to nurse an injury to his throwing thumb. They’ll face a challenge against the Cowboys, who are just 2-2 but look like slim favorites in the NFC East while the Eagles struggle to get out of neutral. The Cowboys have gotten an excellent first four games from Dak Prescott, who has paced one of the most efficient offenses in football. No team is scoring more than Dallas’ 3.4 points per offensive series, and it’s been Prescott and the passing game doing most of that work. (Nearly 75%t of Dallas’ yards have come through the air, compared to a league average of two-thirds.) A big outing against Tampa Bay would solidify the Cowboys’ path to a division title. United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream with NOW or NFL Game Pass on DAZN. Jerry Jones loves a splashy deal, and he made one before last week’s win over the Texans. The Cowboys sent out a package built around a second-round draft choice to bring in Steelers cornerback Joey Porter, who didn’t make a Pro Bowl in his first four seasons but established himself as one of the league’s tougher man-to-man cover players all the same. The next touchdown Porter surrenders as the primary defender on a target will be the first of his career. Dallas made the deal without giving Porter the new contract that had eluded him in Pittsburgh, suggesting Jones saw his acquisition as a win-now endeavor. The Bucs will ride for another week, at least, with rookie QB Jalon Daniels. The Kansas product made his debut in Week 4 and finished 27th of the league’s 32 QBs in passer rating that week, and dead last in yardage per attempt. He sprinkled in a pair of interceptions — not an ideal start for a rookie who is about to turn 24 and whose six years of collegiate experience might have suggested a less rocky debut. Will Daniels find it hospitable to go up against the team that is dead-last in the NFL in net yards allowed per passing attempt (8) through the first four weeks? Tampa Bay’s last flickers of hope depend on it.

At issue is whether the administration can lawfully strip Harvard of federal funding and its ability to enroll international students. By 

                    Josh Moody Harvard, led by President Alan Garber (right), is facing several lawsuits from the Trump administration, which has sought to cut billions in federal funding from the university. Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images | APCortizasJr/iStock/Getty Images | Joseph Prezioso/AFP/Getty Images Harvard University’s sprawling legal battle with the federal government is still grinding on. The private Massachusetts university and the Trump administration met twice in federal appeals court this week as Harvard attempted to repel efforts to cut off billions in research funding and restrict international enrollment. While Harvard picked up wins in the lower courts last year, the Trump administration appealed those rulings. On Monday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit heard arguments in Harvard’s case against the Department of Health and Human Services and other federal agencies over their attempt to cancel more than $2 billion in federal research funding last year for allegedly failing to address antisemitism on campus. U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs ruled last year that the cuts were unlawful and that the federal government violated the university’s First Amendment rights in withholding the funds. Harvard returned to the First Circuit on Tuesday for another showdown with a federal agency. This time it was with the Department of Homeland Security, which has sought to prevent Harvard from enrolling international students. Harvard also prevailed in that case last year. At issue is whether the administration can lawfully strip Harvard of federal funding and its ability to enroll international students, a fight that has emerged as a test of how far the White House can go in using the power of the federal government to pressure colleges to make changes it wants. The Trump administration used the cudgel of alleged antisemitism at Harvard to go after both its federal research funding and international student enrollment, arguing that the university didn’t sufficiently respond to Jewish students’ reports of discrimination. But on appeal, government lawyers focused on whether Burroughs had the authority to restore the funding. “When you look specifically at the grant terminations, there’s no First Amendment right to money,” Justice Department lawyer Michael K. Velchik told a panel of judges Monday. While Velchik accepted that federal district courts can hear Harvard’s First Amendment claims, he argued that the dispute over restoring terminated grants belonged in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. Velchik’s argument hinged on the idea that restoring canceled research funding effectively amounted to enforcing federal contracts, which he said belonged in another court. But Harvard attorney Paul Clement told the panel of three judges that the university was seeking relief that could not be provided by the Court of Federal Claims. He dismissed the notion that the issue at hand is contractual, arguing that the case is about Harvard’s free speech rights. “These are not claims that really depend on the contract in any particular way,” Clement said. “They are claims to be free from retaliatory discrimination under the First Amendment.” Government attorneys also continued to argue this week that the Trump administration has the authority to withhold funds because—in its view—Harvard has not done enough to address antisemitism on campus. But the judges appeared unswayed by that argument. First Circuit Judge Sandra Lynch noted that the government acted against Harvard before proving claims of pervasive antisemitism on campus. (Separately, the Department of Justice sued Harvard in March over alleged antisemitism. A federal judge dismissed that case in August, finding the Trump administration had not demonstrated ongoing violations of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, a federal law that prohibits antisemitism.) “The claim is that Harvard has been indifferent to antisemitism; there are no findings, there was no investigation, there was simply an announcement: ‘We’re terminating,’ against that backdrop,” Lynch said. “It rather looks like the administration didn’t want to have to cope with what the law and the facts of the case presented under both Title VI and the Constitution [say].” She also questioned why the federal government did not use established Title VI processes to address concerns about alleged antisemitism at Harvard before taking punitive action. Lynch, a Clinton appointee, said that the federal government’s claims that Harvard discriminated against Jewish students and failed to adequately police antisemitism on campus are “the precise topics covered by Title VI.” Despite a prior legal setback, the Trump administration appears intent on blocking Harvard from enrolling international students, who comprise nearly a quarter of its student body, per university data. Trump’s proclamation that would have cut off international student enrollment at Harvard was blocked by Burroughs from taking effect in summer 2025 but also expired on its own in December. Justice Department lawyer Tiberius Davis said the federal government had held off on handing down a second order of the same nature because the judge’s order would prevent it from being enforced, but the idea is still in play. Now the White House is looking to revive the ban if the courts clear the way. “I can’t reveal exact conversations or with who, but I have been told by people with the White House that it’s likely he would reissue,” Davis said Tuesday. But First Circuit Judge Gustavo A. Gelpí, a Biden appointee, questioned how such a policy would eliminate antisemitism when it would also bar students from Israel from attending Harvard. title: Climate and SCOTUS: UCLA experts on Suncor v. Boulder - UCLA

Climate took center stage at the Supreme Court on Oct. 5, when the justices heard oral arguments in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County — a case UCLA environmental law experts are closely watching. While the city and county of Boulder are suing oil companies Suncor and Exxon for damages from climate change-related disasters, that’s not the issue before the Supreme Court. The court could rule on Suncor and Exxon’s argument that federal law effectively prevents the case (and dozens of cases like it) from going forward in state courts. title: Honda Reportedly Delays Production of the Next-Gen CR-V Hybrid Until April 2027 - Car and Driver
content: Next-generation CR-Vs will enter production three months late, but they’ll eventually take over the Civic’s spot in Honda’s Indiana plant. The Honda CR-V is getting a major redesign for 2028, but the automaker is reportedly pushing back the start of production to make more 2027 models first. Though the delayed start date means lower output of the new CR-V in the first year, Honda is clearing space for increased production in the near future, according to a report from Automotive News. The CR-V is Honda’s most popular nameplate in the United States, making up 9.5 percent of Honda’s total U.S. sales through September this year. The Civic comes in second place, but Honda is prioritizing U.S. production of the redesigned compact SUV over its economy car in 2028. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 50307 Last year, Honda shifted a lot of its CR-V production from Canada to the United States to lower the impact of import tariffs. U.S.-market CR-Vs are now primarily built in East Liberty, Ohio, and Greensburg, Indiana. The current-generation CR-Vs are in high demand, so Honda is reportedly pushing production of the redesigned hybrid-only CR-V to April 2027 to give this year’s model a bit more production time. The delay means Honda is said to be expecting a 6.7 percent decrease in its monthly output of the redesigned model in its first year. However, that reduction will be followed by a huge production increase. The AN report says Honda is canceling its original plans to build the next-gen Civic at its Indiana plant beginning in May 2028, which gives the CR-V plenty of breathing room once the Civic moves out. The Indiana plant is projected to build around 70,000 Civics this year. Civic hatchbacks sold in North America are exclusively built in Indiana. While the next-gen Civic sedan will still be built in Canada, Honda will begin importing Civic hatchbacks from its Japanese plant once next-gen production takes over. The restructuring is part of Honda’s ambitious plan to release 15 new or heavily refreshed models globally by 2030, with an emphasis on its next-generation hybrid powertrains. Honda is reportedly planning to build another hybrid-focused assembly plant in the United States, but that space is likely claimed by its upcoming large hybrid SUV lineup. The next-generation CR-V will reportedly be sold with only a hybrid powertrain and is projected to start production in 2027 for the 2028 model year.
